summary:
Karaman is a province of Turkey and stands under the national framework: no Karaman-specific statute, incident, or court case appears in the sources behind this record, and the province's exposure is defined by country-wide policy and enforcement practice. That framework has moved from residual prejudice to documented state direction. Kaos GL's 2025 review records hostility toward LGBTI+ people becoming explicit state policy, including "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions.

The most consequential instrument is a leaked omnibus draft, the "11th Judicial Package", reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years' imprisonment, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, subject to mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment underground while exposing people to arrest and pretrial detention. The measure had not been passed as of reporting.

Non-passage has not stopped enforcement. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue those checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detained woman stated that no fines were issued but that the police documented everyone present, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as it was already being applied to them. Turkey also requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Any checkpoint interaction is therefore an occasion on which a visitor's documents can be compared against presentation, with a direct outing risk where appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

Recorded violence is lethal and the state response asymmetric. Kaos GL documents six right-to-life violations in 2025, three of them hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected group. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was referred for arrest. Rights organisations treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Branches of the Human Rights Association in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary and heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
tangentialFactors:
The 2025 monitoring totals indicate the tempo a visitor enters: roughly 313 recorded violations overall, about 2.5 times the previous year, alongside 299 detention decisions. Freedom-of-expression violations rose from 216 to 540, and 89 torture or ill-treatment violations were recorded against 51 the prior year. Censorship extends to artistic events, which have been cancelled or banned, and an LGBTI+ association was closed for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members.

Pride gatherings remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. The Erdoğan government's stated framing of protecting "the family" and "public morals" is identified by Human Rights Watch as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people.

The depth of the pattern predates the current cycle. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robseries and abuse against gay men and transgender people; it is historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than a statement of current law, and it predates the legal changes made after 2018.

outOfScopeNotes:
No statute, incident, police action, court case or healthcare denial specific to Karaman appears in the sources for this record; the province's profile is derived entirely from national instruments and monitoring, and Karaman-level enforcement of GBT checks, document rules or the pending draft is not sourced here.

The 11th Judicial Package was a leaked draft as of the October 2025 reporting and had not been passed; whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn is unresolved in the available material. The same applies to the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation, whose implementation status in Karaman is not stated.

The claim that GBT checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights is attributed to legal experts cited in reporting and has not been confirmed by a ruling in the sources. Whether foreign visitors in Karaman face the same checkpoint frequency documented for Istanbul is unresolved. The Prison Insider and Kaos GL material describes national prison and monitoring conditions and does not identify any facility holding a person from Karaman.
